rule.description: A production method contains a statement sequence run-equivalent to another production method's entire implementation under one consistent bijective renaming of local identifiers instead of delegating to it. Fragments nested inside other matched fragments yield the inlining depth of the container.

checks.description: Detect one production method embedding a whole copy of another production method's body inside its own body, in place of delegating to that method.
checks.detected_relation: container method -> inlined whole body of a lower-level helper method
checks.why_this_is_the_smell: Higher-level orchestration (record synchronization, legacy batch update, WAF cleanup, provider dispatch) silently absorbs lower-level implementations (HTTP request plumbing, listing, filtering, endpoint construction, per-entry commits, socket-based detection), collapsing the abstraction levels that the helper methods established and duplicating their maintenance burden.

excluded.reason: Test-only code is outside the rule's production scope and is skipped by the checker.
Single-statement helper (one for-loop); below the rule's two-statement materiality threshold and trivially reproduced by ordinary iteration, so embedding it is not a meaningful abstraction loss.
Both bodies are built around mid-loop early returns; a whole-body copy cannot preserve that control flow when embedded inside another method, so the relation cannot genuinely occur.

Same early-return structure; also a transport primitive already below any orchestration container in this crate, so absorbing it would model feature inlining rather than the helper-implementation relation.
Leaf string/expression utilities (FQDN construction, proxied-expression parsing) with no subordinate service-method layer; no delegation chain exists to absorb.

Thin composition points over config, provider selection, and the top-level update entry calls; they contain no duplicated sub-method implementation layers, and absorbing their callees would model whole-feature inlining rather than the assigned relation.
